strengths: The paper delivers strong, convincing system-level results on ImageNet 256×256: SVG-XL achieves gFID 3.36–3.94 with only 25 sampling steps at 500–1400 epochs, substantially outperforming DiT/SiT baselines that need 250+ steps, and shows large gains under very few-step sampling (e.g., 12.26 vs 69.38 FID-50K at 5 steps).

The motivation is well-argued and empirically supported: the t-SNE visualization of semantic entanglement in VAE latent spaces and the toy example on velocity-field dispersion give intuitive and testable evidence for why semantically structured latent spaces ease diffusion training and enable few-step sampling.

The proposed design is simple, well-motivated, and ablated: freezing the DINOv3 encoder, adding a lightweight Residual Encoder, and aligning residual features to the DINO distribution are each validated in Table 4 (gFID degrades 6.12→9.03 without distribution alignment), and the choice of VFM is justified by comparisons against SigLIP2, MAE, and DINOv2.

The unified-feature-space claim is backed by actual downstream evaluations (ImageNet-1K classification, ADE20K segmentation, NYUv2 depth) showing the SVG space preserves DINOv3's discriminative capability, plus qualitative evidence (editing, interpolation, PCA feature maps).

Training and inference efficiency gains are significant and clearly reported (Figure 1: ~35–62× speedups), which is practically important for the LDM community; hyperparameters, compute, and sampler details are disclosed, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty positioning is questionable. The core idea—training diffusion models directly on frozen DINO-style features with a lightweight decoder/adapter to restore reconstruction fidelity—closely overlaps with recent concurrent work (e.g., Representation Autoencoders (RAE), REPA-E, 'Diffuse and Disperse', which the paper cites). The claim of being the 'first' to repurpose self-supervised features for generative modeling appears overstated; the paper should provide a sharper delta analysis against these methods rather than dismissing them as 'ad hoc fixes'.

The 'without VAE' framing is somewhat misleading: the SVG decoder still follows the VAE decoder design and is trained with the LDM reconstruction objective, and a residual encoder-adapter is trained per dataset. What is removed is the VAE encoder, not the autoencoding machinery, so the practical benefit over a well-regularized VAE or feature-space tokenizer needs clearer delineation.

Comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: key baseline numbers (SiT-XL under VA-VAE) are the authors' own reproductions, baselines are evaluated at 80 epochs while the best SVG numbers use 500–1400 epochs, and REPA-XL at full training reports gFID 1.42 with CFG—far better than SVG's 2.10 (w/ CFG)—which weakens the 'surpassing SOTA' narrative if raw generative quality is the metric.

Classifier-free guidance is admitted to be less effective in this framework (limitation section), yet all headline comparisons with CFG baselines (e.g., Table 1) still use CFG for SVG; the reasons for degraded CFG effectiveness and the impact on fair comparison deserve more analysis.

Scope is narrow: everything is class-conditional ImageNet 256×256. There is no evidence on text-to-image, higher resolutions, or larger datasets—precisely the settings where the unified-representation argument would be most compelling. The limitations section acknowledges this, but it caps the significance.

Some analysis is suggestive rather than rigorous: the link between semantic dispersion and few-step sampling quality is supported by t-SNE plots and a toy example but lacks quantitative corroboration (e.g., velocity-field consistency metrics); downstream probing uses only lightweight linear/FPN decoders against a single DINOv3 baseline, so 'task-generality' is asserted on a limited basis. Single-run results without variance estimates further reduce confidence.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper provides an intuitive analysis (t-SNE visualizations and a toy velocity-field example) of why semantically entangled VAE latents hinder diffusion training, and connects this to recent VFM-alignment trends (REPA, VA-VAE, REPA-E).

The proposed method is simple and sensible: freezing DINOv3 features, adding a lightweight residual encoder for perceptual detail, and aligning residual outputs to the DINO feature distribution is a clean design, and the ablation in Table 4 shows each component matters (gFID degrades from 6.12 to 9.03 without distribution alignment).

Strong empirical results on ImageNet 256x256: gFID 3.36 (w/o CFG) / 1.92 (w/ CFG) at 25 sampling steps after 1400 epochs, with good few-step behavior (12.26 FID-50K at 5 steps) and consistent advantages across model scales (Table 2b).

The dual evaluation of generation plus downstream perception tasks (ImageNet classification, ADE20K segmentation, NYUv2 depth) and qualitative analyses (editing, interpolation, PCA feature maps) support the 'unified feature space' narrative better than most tokenizer papers.
The paper is generally well written, with hyperparameters (Table 5), training details, and appendices that make the work reasonably reproducible.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is a serious concern. The headline '62x faster' is computed against SiT-XL with SD-VAE, but the paper's own Table 1 shows SiT-XL with VA-VAE achieves 5.96/3.63 gFID at 250 steps and 7.29/4.13 at 25 steps — very close to SVG-XL's 6.57/3.54 at 80 epochs. Against the closest, properly matched baseline, the actual margin is small, and the efficiency claims are substantially overstated.

Novelty is incremental. The core idea is essentially the next step in the REPA/VA-VAE/REPA-E line: replace 'align VAE latents to VFM features' with 'directly use VFM features plus a residual encoder.' Given DINOv3's extremely strong pretrained representation (trained on massive proprietary-scale data), it is unsurprising that diffusion on top of it trains faster; the paper benefits enormously from an external foundation model that baselines do not get to exploit, and the contribution of the paper itself (a residual encoder + distribution alignment) is modest.

The 'unified/task-general feature space' claim is largely inherited rather than earned: DINOv3 already achieves the reported downstream results, and Table 4 shows SVG's perception gains over DINOv3 are marginal (e.g., 46.51 vs 46.37 mIoU). The tokenization adds little to understanding capability.

The central analysis is qualitative and anecdotal. The t-SNE plots and toy two-class example do not constitute rigorous evidence that semantic dispersion is the causal driver of training efficiency; no quantitative correlation, controlled latent-space manipulation, or ablation isolates this mechanism.

The latent space is much higher-dimensional (16x16x384) than VAE latents (32x32x4), yet a detailed compute/throughput accounting (training FLOPs, wall-clock per epoch, memory) is missing, making the efficiency story hard to verify beyond the epoch-based comparisons, which are not throughput-equivalent.

The approach is confined to class-conditional ImageNet generation; text-to-image, higher resolution, and the very settings where the unified-representation claim would matter most are deferred to future work. The paper also admits CFG is less effective in its framework, which is a practical limitation left unresolved.

Some claims lack support: 'for the first time demonstrate that features learned via self-supervised methods can be directly repurposed for generative modeling' ignores closely related prior work (e.g., representation-generation methods the paper itself cites, such as Li et al. 2023b).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper identifies semantic entanglement in VAE latent spaces as a bottleneck for latent diffusion training, supported by t-SNE visualizations and an intuitive toy example on velocity-field dispersion.

The proposed SVG design is simple and elegant: a frozen DINOv3 encoder combined with a lightweight Residual Encoder and distribution alignment, preserving semantic discriminability while adding the perceptual detail needed for faithful reconstruction.

Strong empirical results: SVG-XL achieves gFID 1.92 (w/ CFG) in only 25 sampling steps, competitive with or better than DiT/SiT/REPA baselines that use 250 steps, and shows a large few-step sampling advantage (e.g., 12.26 vs 69.38 FID at 5 steps w/o CFG).

Convincing evidence that the feature space is task-general: downstream ImageNet-1K classification, ADE20K segmentation, and NYUv2 depth results match or slightly exceed DINOv3, unlike prior tokenizer-focused work.

Good ablation coverage: choice of VFM, contribution of the Residual Encoder, effect of distribution alignment (gFID 9.03 -> 6.11), model scaling across B/L/XL, and analyses of editing, interpolation, and feature-map structure.
Comparison tables include both with/without CFG, reproduce baselines (SiT† with VA-VAE) under matched settings, and report wall-clock/epoch efficiency, improving fairness and transparency.
Honest limitations section acknowledging reduced CFG effectiveness, unexplored T2I/T2V, and high-dimensional latents; LLM assistance is properly disclosed.
weaknesses: Scope limited to class-conditional ImageNet 256x256; no text-to-image or higher-resolution experiments, so claims about 'unified visual representations' and broader impact are not yet fully validated.

Heavy dependence on a frozen DINOv3 encoder trained on large proprietary data; the 'no VAE / self-supervised latent space' contribution partly offloads representation learning to a strong external VFM, which weakens the self-containedness of the contribution and raises questions about generalization to settings without such an encoder.

The headline '62x faster' comparisons mix training epochs and sampling steps in ways that are not strictly apples-to-apples (SVG at 25 steps vs baselines at 250 steps with different tokenizers); a compute-matched (GPU-hours) comparison would be more convincing.

The central claim that semantic dispersion causes efficient diffusion training is supported mainly by qualitative t-SNE plots and a toy example; a quantitative correlation (e.g., feature-space metrics vs training efficiency) would strengthen the causal argument.

The 16x16x384 latent space is high-dimensional relative to 16x16x4 VAE latents; while training is stable, inference FLOPs/memory and potential for dimensionality reduction are not thoroughly analyzed.

Some baseline gaps: no comparison against newer unified-representation or distillation-based few-step methods, and REPA-XL's 800-epoch result (gFID 1.42) is not directly discussed in the main comparison.
CFG is markedly less effective in the proposed space (and requires the zero-init trick); the mechanism behind this is not analyzed in depth.

Notation/typos (e.g., inconsistent DINO vs DINOv2/v3 citation for 'Zhang et al., 2022', eq. 2/5 missing norm bars) and some claims ('for the first time') that could be softened given closely related work (REPA, RCG, DC-AE-style tokenizers).

strengths: Strong empirical results: SVG-XL achieves gFID 3.36 (w/o CFG) / 1.92 (w/ CFG) in only 25 sampling steps, outperforming DiT/SiT/REPA baselines at comparable or fewer training epochs, with consistent advantages across model scales (B/L/XL) and few-step regimes (5/10/25 steps).

Comprehensive evaluation: system-level comparisons on ImageNet 256×256, few-step generation, model scaling, ablations of the residual encoder and distribution alignment (Table 4), downstream transfer tasks (classification, segmentation, depth), zero-shot editing, latent interpolation, and higher-resolution (512/1024) scaling.

The motivating analysis (t-SNE of VAE latent spaces in Fig. 4a and the toy velocity-field example in Fig. 4b) provides an intuitive account of why semantically dispersed latent spaces ease diffusion training and few-step sampling, going beyond purely empirical gains.

The paper is generally well-written and the two-stage training pipeline (residual encoder + distribution alignment) is simple and clearly described, with sufficient implementation details (hyperparameters, compute, sampler, CFG settings) for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim is overstated. The paper claims to demonstrate 'for the first time' that self-supervised features can be directly repurposed for generative modeling, but RCG (Li et al., 2023b), which the paper itself cites, already trains a diffusion model in a self-supervised representation space with a light decoder to pixels, and REG (Wang & He, 2025) pursues a closely related direction. No quantitative comparison against RCG/REG is provided, which weakens the positioning.

Unfair comparison baseline concern: SVG inherits a frozen DINOv3 encoder pretrained on massive external data (and distilled from a 7B model), whereas baseline tokenizers (SD-VAE, VA-VAE) are trained only on ImageNet. The gains may substantially reflect the transferred pretrained knowledge rather than the proposed feature-space design. Ablations isolating this effect (e.g., a randomly initialized encoder or ImageNet-only DINO) are missing.

The core hypothesis—that semantic dispersion enables efficient diffusion—is supported mainly by t-SNE visualizations and a 2-class toy example, not by rigorous analysis (e.g., quantitative correlation between linear-probe accuracy and gFID across many latent spaces). The mechanism for improved few-step sampling (reduced discretization error) remains heuristic.

The distribution alignment in Eq. (6) uses only batch statistics of the residual features to match DINO feature statistics; per-channel moment matching may not preserve the DINO distribution outside the training distribution, and its robustness at inference time is not analyzed.

The authors themselves acknowledge that classifier-free guidance is less effective in their framework (best gFID 3.36 at a low CFG scale of 1.5, with performance degrading at larger scales per Fig. 13), which is a notable limitation for the generative quality claims.

Scope is limited to class-conditional ImageNet generation; no text-to-image or video results, despite the abstract positioning SVG as a step toward 'task-general' representations. Latent dimensionality (16×16×384 vs. 32×32×4 for VAE) is high; the promised reduction in dimensionality is left as future work.

Project page and code repository fields are empty at submission time, and some reproduced baseline numbers (e.g., SiT-XL with VA-VAE) cannot be verified, somewhat limiting reproducibility and verifiability of the headline '62×/35× faster' claims.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental suite: system-level comparison on ImageNet 256x256, few-step generation, model scaling, encoder ablations (Table 3), component ablations (Table 4), downstream transfer (classification, segmentation, depth), and efficiency profiling (Table 7).

The core results are impressive: SVG-XL reaches gFID 3.36 (w/o CFG) in only 25 steps, substantially better than SiT/VA-VAE baselines at comparable or longer training, and downstream performance is essentially preserved relative to frozen DINOv3.

The analysis of semantic dispersion in VAE latent spaces (t-SNE in Fig. 4a, toy velocity-field example in Fig. 4b) is a reasonable motivating study, and the distribution-alignment ablation (6.12 -> 9.03 -> 6.11 gFID) cleanly validates the alignment component.
Hyperparameters, training details, and compute (8xH100) are reported in the appendix, supporting partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: Overclaiming novelty: the claim of being 'the first to demonstrate that self-supervised features can be repurposed for generative modeling' is inaccurate. RCG (Li et al., 2023b), Diffuse & Disperse (Wang & He, 2025), REPA (Yu et al., 2025), and VA-VAE already pursue closely related ideas (representation-guided generation or aligning latents/hidden states to SSL features). The contribution is an incremental combination of these: DINO latents + residual encoder + batch-statistics alignment (Eq. 6 is a simple per-feature standardization).

Serious potential confound: the 'tokenizer' is built on a frozen DINOv3 encoder pretrained by Meta on very large, partially undisclosed data that likely includes ImageNet-1K-like content. This could inflate both reconstruction and downstream 'unified representation' results, and the paper does not discuss or control for this leakage. The comparison against VAEs trained only on ImageNet is not apples-to-apples.

The method's success hinges heavily on one specific, very recent encoder (DINOv3). The encoder comparison (Table 3) covers only a few alternatives and does not establish generality of the recipe; a DINOv2-based SVG with the residual encoder under the same protocol would strengthen the claim, but is missing.

Reproducibility is weak in practice: the Project Page and Code Repository fields are empty. For a systems-heavy paper whose central artifact (SVG tokenizer) depends on a particular pretrained checkpoint, missing code materially undermines verification.

Evidence for the key mechanistic claim (semantic dispersion -> easier/faster diffusion, fewer sampling steps) is largely qualitative: a single toy example with two classes (Fig. 4b) and t-SNE plots. No quantitative measure of latent structure correlated with gFID or step count is provided, leaving the causal story under-supported.

CFG is notably less effective in this framework (cfg 1.55-1.5, and acknowledged in limitations), and the w/o CFG numbers, while good, are the ones mostly compared against baselines' w/ CFG results in Table 2; some comparisons across different guidance settings reduce clarity of the advantage.

Scope is limited to class-conditional ImageNet generation; the 'task-general, unified feature space' framing (and text-to-image ambitions) is not substantiated beyond frozen-encoder linear probing, and the residual branch concatenation means the latent is DINO-dominant rather than genuinely unified.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated analysis of why VAE latent spaces are suboptimal for latent diffusion, supported by t-SNE visualizations (Figure 4a), a toy example of velocity-field structure (Figure 4b), and PCA visualizations of diffusion hidden states (Appendix G), which together give an intuitive and plausible account of how semantic discriminability in the latent space accelerates diffusion training.

The empirical results are strong: SVG-XL achieves gFID=3.36 (w/o CFG) / 1.92 (w/ CFG) with only 25 sampling steps and strong few-step performance (5 and 10 steps, Table 2a), significantly outperforming SiT with both SD-VAE and VA-VAE tokenizers under matched epochs.

Comprehensive evaluation beyond generation: downstream transfer (ImageNet-1K classification, ADE20K segmentation, NYUv2 depth, Table 4), model scaling behavior (Table 2b), zero-shot editing, interpolation tests, tokenizer efficiency (Table 7), encoder-layer ablations (Table 6), and higher-resolution experiments (Appendix H).

The design is simple and well-ablated: the residual encoder with batch-statistics distribution alignment (Eq. 6) is shown to be essential via Table 4 (naive concatenation degrades gFID from 6.12 to 9.03).
The paper is generally well written and organized, with detailed implementation and hyperparameter information in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated. The claim of being 'the first time' self-supervised features are repurposed for generative modeling ignores closely related work the paper itself cites: RCG (Li et al., 2023b) generates self-supervised representations; REPA/REPA-E (Yu et al., 2025; Leng et al., 2025) and VA-VAE (Yao et al., 2025) already align diffusion representations or VAE latents with DINO/VFM features. The core delta—using frozen DINOv3 features directly as the diffusion target plus a residual encoder—is relatively incremental.

Comparison fairness concerns: the method fundamentally depends on DINOv3, an extremely strong, large-scale pretrained external model, whereas baselines use VAE tokenizers. Additionally, REPA-XL still achieves a better w/ CFG gFID (1.42 at 800 epochs) than SVG-XL (2.10 at 500 epochs; 1.92 at 1400 epochs), so the 'surpasses baselines' claim is only partially supported.

All experiments are limited to class-conditional ImageNet 256x256 generation; the 'task-general / unified feature space' claim rests mostly on matching (not exceeding) frozen DINOv3's downstream performance via simple linear/MLP probes, which is a modest bar and weak evidence of practical unified representation value.

The latent space is very high-dimensional (16x16x384 vs. 16x16x4), and while the authors argue inference is not inefficient, the effect on diffusion model training cost, memory, and scalability is not analyzed in depth.
The authors themselves note CFG is less effective in their framework, and no principled remedy is offered; this limitation affects the headline numbers and generality of the approach.
No code repository or project page is provided (both fields are empty), which limits reproducibility at review time.
